title: Adding jitter inside the backoff kernel gives a pure module a random number generator
summary: The kernels in this module are pure so that a deterministic simulator can drive the whole cluster through thousands of seeded runs and replay any failure exactly. A developer adds jitter to the backoff, the textbook improvement, by calling `ThreadLocalRandom` inside the kernel, and updates the tests to accept a range. The module's capability contract, which lists every JDK capability its bytecode can reach, gains `randomness`, and the build fails: the module can no longer be replayed.

change.description: Subtract a random amount of up to a quarter from each delay, so that peers retrying after the same outage do not retry in lockstep. The randomness comes from `ThreadLocalRandom.current()`, the standard choice. The tests are changed from exact values to ranges and pass. The developer meant to change the delays, not what the module is able to do, so the capability contract is left as it is.

risk: The value of this module is that it is a function: a simulator (in the style of FoundationDB's or TigerBeetle's) runs a seeded cluster of these kernels, injects partitions and clock skew, and when an invariant breaks, replays the seed to the exact step. One call to a random number generator inside a kernel breaks that for every run that reaches a retry: the failure reproduces on the simulator's seed only by luck, and a developer bisecting a once-in-ten-thousand-runs failure loses the tool that found it. The property proof of this method (examples 016) is also lost, since the method is no longer a function of its inputs. Jitter belongs in the scheduler that owns the clock and the seed, outside the kernel.
explanation: The capability contract of the module is derived from its compiled classes: every call from the module's bytecode to a JDK entry point of a capability (the clock, randomness, threads, the network, reflection, ...), grouped by capability. The committed contract says `randomness: none`, which is the module's promise of determinism. The patched bytecode calls `ThreadLocalRandom.current` and `nextLong` from `Backoff.delayMillis`, and the contract check lists both call sites. This is a closed-world check over every instruction, not a lint: bytecode that never names an entry point of a capability cannot exercise it, and the ways around that (reflection, method handles, native code) are capabilities on the list themselves. Deriving it takes milliseconds and needs no JVM.
resolution: Move the jitter to the caller: the kernel returns the undithered delay, and the scheduler, which already owns the clock and the simulator's seeded random source, subtracts a random slice. The kernel stays a function, the capability contract stays empty, and the simulator keeps replaying. If a module really must gain a capability, `jvmcontract update` regenerates the contract and the diff names the new power and the call site, for a reviewer to approve.
provenance: Constructed from the design rule of deterministic-simulation-tested systems that no component below the simulator may read a clock or a random source of its own.
